name: class-table-inheritance
intent: Represent an inheritance hierarchy relationally with one table per class: each table stores only the attributes the class itself declares, and each subclass table's primary key doubles as a foreign key to its superclass table, so every attribute is stored exactly once and the schema itself enforces that every subtype row is also a base-class row.
problem: An object hierarchy has to be persisted relationally and the schema keeps lying about it: shared and subclass-specific attributes either share one wide table full of nullable columns, or every concrete class duplicates the inherited columns. Neither layout can state a subclass attribute as NOT NULL, neither shows which class actually owns a column, and adding a subtype or changing one subtype's attributes forces a schema edit that touches unrelated types.
context: Applies where a relational store holds a genuine IS-A hierarchy that is mapped to objects, the hierarchy has attributes declared at several levels (not just a status flag), and both polymorphic reads by base type and per-subclass integrity matter. It is the middle option between single table inheritance (one table plus a discriminator, cheap reads, nullable subtype columns) and concrete table inheritance (no joins, duplicated base columns), and it fits best where the schema is owned or reviewed — a DBA, a legacy layout, or a regulated data model. ORM-specific names: SQLAlchemy calls this joined table inheritance, JPA/Hibernate calls it JOINED, EF Core calls it TPT (table-per-type).
benefits: Every attribute is stored exactly once, in the table of the class that declares it: no nullable padding for sibling types and no duplicated base columns.
Constraints stay honest: subclass-only columns can be NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECKed and indexed, precisely because no sibling type ever writes to them.
Referential integrity is structural: subclass keys are foreign keys to the superclass table, so an orphaned subtype row cannot exist, and base-table references stay valid for every subtype.
A new subclass adds one table plus its mapper and touches no sibling table or sibling mapper.
Polymorphic reads are natural: a base-class query joins only the paths it needs, while a query restricted to one subclass reads one join path and can use that subclass table's indexes.
The base table alone answers base-class questions, so the cheap common path stays cheap.
Normalized schema satisfies database purists and regulatory audits where nullable columns representing non-applicable attributes are unacceptable.

Each subtype's physical storage is independent: buffer pages, VACUUM schedules, and index maintenance are type-specific, eliminating the lock contention that co-located subtypes create in single-table layouts.
tradeoffs: Every subclass read pays one join per class in its inheritance path; deep hierarchies (more than 3–4 levels) degrade predictably, and EF Core's own modelling guidance warns that table-per-type is slower than table-per-hierarchy.
Insert, update and delete touch every table in the path and must happen in one transaction, or the schema temporarily disagrees with the object.
Polymorphic loading needs a discriminator plus mapper machinery that resolves the concrete class per row; without it you get partially populated objects rather than an error.
The table layout encodes the class structure, so refactoring the hierarchy (pushing a field up or down) becomes a schema migration instead of a code move.
Object identity now spans rows in several tables, which complicates bulk operations, exports, reporting SQL and any code that reaches the database without the mapper.
There is more mapping machinery than the single-table alternative: one mapper per class, a registry of type codes and a join builder, and hand-written queries become harder to read.
The JOIN cost is paid even for leaf-class queries: a query for a leaf subclass that never accesses base-class columns still joins the entire ancestor chain.

participants.responsibility: The domain types whose attributes are partitioned across tables; each class's declared attributes determine which table owns which column.
Holds the attributes declared by the root class plus the shared primary key and, normally, the type code (discriminator) that says which concrete class a row is.
One per subclass; its primary key is also a foreign key to the table of its superclass, and it stores only the attributes that class declares.
Reads and writes the join path for its class, converts rows to objects, and resolves the concrete class from the type code on polymorphic reads (Inheritance Mappers).
The key value that ties the rows of one object across the tables together and gives the object its identity (Identity Field).
A column (usually on the base table) whose value identifies the concrete subclass for each row, enabling the mapper to resolve which class to instantiate on polymorphic reads.

use_cases: A billing hierarchy (payment base table plus credit-card and bank-transfer tables) where each method's columns are mandatory only for that method.
Party models: a shared party table carrying identity, with person and organisation tables holding the type-specific columns.
Product or asset catalogues with a common item table plus per-category attribute tables owned by different teams.
Regulated or DBA-owned schemas that require normalised tables, no nullable type columns and database-enforced foreign keys.
Legacy databases already laid out as one table per class, where new domain classes have to map onto the existing shape.
Deep type trees in which queries usually target one concrete subtype while the base table remains the cheap common lookup.

Multi-tenant SaaS event systems: a shared events table plus per-type extension tables (user_events, billing_events) where type-specific columns must be NOT NULL for their type and where tenant isolation requires per-type foreign keys.

Notification systems: a base notification table (user_id, created_at, read) with EmailNotification and SmsNotification extension tables where channel-specific columns (email_address, phone_number) must be NOT NULL enforced at the database level.
Organisational hierarchies where the base party table is referenced by many other tables, but subtype-specific columns differ significantly across Person, Organisation, and GovernmentAgency.

Django's built-in multi-table inheritance: every child model gets its own table linked to the parent by an implicit OneToOneField, used for hierarchies like Place/Restaurant where each model must stay independently queryable.

Doctrine ORM's JOINED strategy (the Person/Employee example): discriminator column on the root table plus per-class child tables joined by foreign key, chosen when changing one subtype's columns must not touch sibling tables.
Rails apps that outgrow single-table inheritance and move subclass columns into per-type tables via delegated types or the activerecord-cti / class-table-inheritance gems.
avoid_when: The hierarchy is small and stable with few subclass-specific columns: single table inheritance (one table plus a type code) is far simpler and pays no joins.
Reads dominate and almost always load whole hierarchies polymorphically: joining every subclass table costs more than the nullable columns it avoids.
Subclasses add no attributes of their own — the difference is behaviour or a status flag: a type column, or Special Case objects, replaces the hierarchy.
The types only share a few fields but are not an IS-A family: composition (a shared component or Embedded Value) models that better than a mapped hierarchy.
The schema is not yours to shape (third-party or dataset-owned) or the store is not relational: this is a schema-shape decision, not only a mapping decision.
EF Core is the ORM and the hierarchy has more than 5–6 subclasses: EF Core's TPT query generation historically produces extremely complex SQL with many LEFT OUTER JOINs that degrades badly at scale.
Polymorphic queries returning large result sets are the primary access pattern: the per-row joins outweigh the storage savings for most workloads.
anti_patterns: One table per class schemas in which every subclass table also repeats the inherited columns — concrete table inheritance wearing a joined schema's clothes, with the same update anomalies the pattern removes.

Subclass tables with their own separately generated surrogate keys instead of a key that is also a foreign key to the base table: nothing then enforces one-to-one, so duplicated identities and orphan rows appear.
Inventing a new subclass (and table) for every minor behavioural variation, so the schema grows a table per special case and every read joins half the hierarchy.
Loading a subclass through a query that joins only part of its inheritance path and handing out partially populated objects.
Hand-written SQL that reads the base table alone and then assumes subclass columns are present.
Mixing STI and CTI in the same hierarchy without clear boundaries: the polymorphic query planner receives a mix of nullable columns and joined tables that cannot be optimised effectively.
Using CTI for a hierarchy where subtypes are queried together (polymorphically) more than 80% of the time — the joins outweigh every other benefit.
design_principles: Single source of truth: each attribute is stored once, where the class declares it.
Open/closed: a new subclass extends the schema and the mapper set without editing existing mappers.
Separation of concerns: keys, attribute storage and mapping knowledge are separate, and domain classes stay ignorant of the tables.
Integrity by construction: making the subclass key a foreign key states the one-to-one invariant the object model assumes.
Liskov substitution at the data level: a subtype row is a base-table row, so references to the base table remain valid for every subtype.
Query cost is proportional to data accessed: only the tables involved in a query contribute to its cost; base-table-only queries never pay subclass join penalties.
best_practices: Let the base table own the primary key and the discriminator/type code; make every subclass table's primary key a foreign key to its superclass's table (PK = FK).
Index the discriminator column on the base table; index each subclass table's FK column (the shared key) since it is the join key on every polymorphic query.
Write all tables of a path in one transaction — base row first on insert, leaf row first on delete — or let ON DELETE CASCADE clean up the path.
Keep one mapper per class (Inheritance Mappers) and let it own the join path for that class so the join is written once.
Load subclass-only columns only when the query needs them; a base-class query should not pay for subclass joins it does not use.
Keep subclass column names disjoint from the names in their superclass tables, since name-resolved mappers and hand-written readers confuse them.
Record the mapping (class to table and to type code) as metadata or configuration instead of re-deriving it in each mapper.
Prefer shallow hierarchies (3 or fewer levels): each level adds one JOIN to every leaf-class query; beyond 3 levels the join cost becomes measurable.
For SQLAlchemy: configure polymorphic_load='selectin' on leaf subclasses to eliminate N+1 lazy-load queries; use selectin_polymorphic() for bulk base-class queries.
For Hibernate/JPA: add @BatchSize(size=25) on subclass entities to batch lazy-loads; consider a discriminator column even for JOINED to let Hibernate skip the CASE WHEN EXISTS subqueries.
For EF Core: only use TPT when NOT NULL constraints on subclass columns are a hard requirement; otherwise prefer TPH; always review generated SQL with EXPLAIN/ANALYZE.
Use bulk operations (COPY, batch insert) at the appropriate level: insert base rows in bulk, then subclass rows in bulk — never interleave them.
For polymorphic reporting queries across the full hierarchy, consider a denormalised read replica or a materialized view rather than repeated multi-join queries.
pitfalls: N+1 lazy-load queries: the default behavior when loading a base class is to NOT join subclass tables, so accessing subclass attributes triggers one SELECT per row. Fix with eager loading (selectin_polymorphic in SQLAlchemy, @BatchSize in Hibernate).
Deep hierarchy join amplification: a 5-level hierarchy pays 4 joins per leaf query regardless of which leaf; plan the hierarchy depth deliberately.
Bulk delete without proper ordering: deleting from subclass tables before the base table violates FK constraints unless ON DELETE CASCADE is used — always delete from base or use CASCADE.
Discriminator drift: if the application code sets the discriminator column directly rather than through the ORM mapper, wrong type codes cause object instantiation failures at runtime.
Cross-ORM polymorphic associations: a relationship from a CTI-mapped entity to the base class that is then loaded through a different ORM session can return partially-loaded objects.
Schema drift during refactoring: moving a field up or down the class hierarchy is a multi-table migration, not a code move — plan migrations with backward compatibility windows.
Key generation strategy mismatch: using TABLE/GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY on the base table but sequences or UUIDs on subclasses breaks the PK=FK invariant unless the same generator is used.
Partial index on base table columns: a partial index on base columns filtered by discriminator can be bypassed by ORM polymorphic queries that rewrite the filter incorrectly.
EF Core TPT query plan bloat: EF Core's TPT query generation can produce query plans with hundreds of joins at scale, which is an EF Core limitation, not a fundamental CTI problem.

Wrong move: mapping 30+ sibling subclasses onto one JOINED base entity -> every polymorphic base query fans out into a join per subclass, hitting MySQL's 61-table join limit and collapsing the query plan -> instead collapse sibling leaf types (SINGLE_TABLE with secondary tables keeps the per-type columns) or split the hierarchy into separate roots.

Wrong move: defining a ForeignKey on a Django multi-table inheritance child model without an explicit related_name -> the implicit parent-link reverse accessor collides and system checks fail -> instead set related_name on every relation declared in a child model.

Wrong move: using Doctrine partial objects to dodge JOINED joins -> any later access to a field outside the partial selection returns an incomplete object or triggers hidden reloads -> instead keep hot polymorphic fields on the root table or explicitly join the subtype tables the query reads.
